description_block:
Armand Guillaumin
(French, 1841-1927)
Rivière à Crozant (Le Moulin Bouchardon)
oil on canvas
signed Guillaumin (lower right)

25 3/4 x 32 in. (65.4 x 81.3 cm)

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
The present lot is currently under review for authenticity by the Comité Guillaumin.Provenance:Galerie de la Présidence, Paris.Acquired directly from the above by the present owner.Private Collection. Lot Note:Rivière à Crozant (Le Moulin Bouchardon), was painted in Crozant, located in the Creuse region, central France, and a subject that Armand Guillaumin revisited in his oils on numerous occasions. As in the present work, many of the Crozant paintings feature the dam associated with the Bouchardon mill, located along the Creuse River. Guillaumin was a leader of the École de Crozant, a loose group of artists who depicted landscapes in the Creuse region. More importantly, he was also a founding member of the Impressionist movement, painting alongside Paul Cézanne, Camille Pissarro, and Pierre-Auguste Renoir among others.Guillaumin's path to becoming an artist was far from ordinary. His interest began at a young age while living in Moulins, but from the time he moved to Paris in 1857 until 1891, he had to put work before painting in order to earn a living. His jobs ranged from being a clerk in his uncle's lingerie shop, to working for the Paris-Orléans railroad, to taking evening shifts digging for the Highway Department. Despite the hard work, he painted throughout and exhibited at the Salon des Refusés in 1863, along with a group of artists soon to be dubbed the "Impressionists" and participated in six of the eight Impressionist group shows. Guillaumin was also a close friend of Vincent van Gogh, with whom he had in common paintings featuring bold coloration combined with painterly brushwork, as in the present lot. In 1891, Guillaumin was finally able to quit his day job and concentrate on painting full-time when he won 100,000 francs in the state lottery. This money allowed him to settle permanently in the Creuse region. Much like Claude Monet, who likewise painted in the area, Guillaumin often painted in the same locale, in different atmospheric conditions and at different times of day. In the present painting, the view shows the mill in the background, partially hidden by the river’s lush foliage, with the autumnal environment conveyed through brilliant pinks, violets, and oranges laid down with thick, energetic brushstrokes. Other examples of the same scene but from varying perspectives include The Bouchardon Mill, Crozant, c. 1898 (Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York) and The Bouchardon Mill, Crozant, c. 1894 (Philadelphia Museum of Art).What remained consistent through Guillaumin’s landscapes in Crozant is the almost complete lack of any human life and presence, as if the landscape was enough, contrary to his earlier cityscapes. Similar to Monet, Guillaumin was equally fascinated by the region, as it represented to both of them the purest form of Nature, an area where modernity, progress, and industrialization had not yet invaded. The landscape offered dramatic, isolated views in which the artist could paint transcendental depictions of nature through expressive use of contrasting colors and gestural brushwork. The works, including the present painting, would go on to considerably influence the forthcoming Post-Impressionist artists. His evolving technique, from the early realistic period to his Impressionist approach, placed him as a key figure in the development of early 20th century painting.

description_block:
Lyonel Feininger
(American, 1871-1956)
Houses in Kromsdorf, Weimar, 1953
ink wash and ink on paper
signed Feininger (lower left), titled (lower center), and dated 29. VIII. '53 (lower right); inscribed KROMSDORF (verso)

sheet: 16 7/8 x 12 3/8 in. (42.9 x 31.4 cm)

Property from a Distinguished Private Collection

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Achim Moeller, Managing Principal of The Lyonel Feininger Project LLC, New York – Berlin has confirmed the authenticity of this work, which is registered under no. 1891-01-30-24. A certificate of authenticity accompanies the work. Additional information was provided by Achim Moeller, The Lyonel Feininger Project LLC, New York – Berlin. Provenance:Willard Gallery, New York.Acquired directly from the above in 1956.Private Collection, New York.Exhibited:New York, Willard Gallery, A Group of Exceptional Drawings, January 3 - 28, 1956, no. 5 (as Kromsdorf), n.p.Lot Note:The present drawing shows a street in Kromsdorf, a village three miles northeast of Weimar in Thuringia. It is one of the hamlets Feininger explored by bicycle in the years before the First World War. He first recorded the motif in a pencil sketch on May 23, 1913, one of the rapid Natur-Notizen, or "nature notes," that served as the raw material for his paintings. From it came a charcoal drawing in 1914 and two canvases, Großkromsdorf II (1915; Moeller 161) and Großkromsdorf III (1921; Moeller 232).Forty years after that first sketch, Feininger returned to the motif in New York. He had settled there after leaving Germany in 1937 and never went back. He had long trusted such notes to hold an image in reserve. As early as 1906 he wrote to his future wife, Julia, that "the image lies within the note itself."¹ Houses in Kromsdorf bears out that conviction: a village street, set down in minutes in 1913, still yields a composition four decades later. Even the inscription, written in English, measures the distance between the place and the man remembering it.The sheet shows the hallmarks of his late graphic style. Broad passages of rubbed charcoal establish volume and atmosphere. Over them runs a scaffolding of fine, broken ink lines, ruled and stippled, that holds the gabled houses within a lattice of intersecting planes. The steep roofs and blank façades remain legible, yet they dissolve at their edges into light. The result is less a view than a crystallized memory, true to Feininger's conviction that what one sees "must be transformed in the mind."Made just over two years before his death, the drawing completes a motif that runs from 1913 to 1953. It joins the Thuringian village studies that formed his mature vision to the luminous, spectral architectures of his final decade.

Fernand Léger

Les Constructeurs au Vélo, 1950
gouache on paper

Property from a Private Collection. 

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
This lot has been authenticated by the Comité Léger and will be accompanied by a certificate of authenticity.Provenance:Collection of Daniel Wallard.Lot Note:In the early 1950s, Fernand Léger began working on Les Constructeurs, one of the most important series of his late career. Reflecting on post-war Europe’s reconstruction, it also focused on the dignity of working-class labor and the scale of modern industry. Among its key preparatory works is the 1950 gouache Les Constructeurs au Vélo, which Freeman’s will proudly offer for sale in its October 27 Impressionist & Modern Art auction in New York.Léger’s inspiration came during his evening drives to Chevreuse, where he saw construction workers climbing newly erected high-voltage pylons. He recalled being struck by the contrast between the small scale of the workers and the rigid industrial structures around them: “Lost in the rigid, hard, hostile surroundings, the men appeared tiny. I wanted to render this in my paintings, without making any concessions.”Les Constructeurs au Vélo brings together the central elements of the series. The lower half is organized around the workers, while the upper half is dominated by intersecting metal structures. A bicycle in the foreground refers to everyday working-class life and mobility. The work also connects Léger’s early interest in Cubism and mechanical forms with his later focus on labor and collective life. Here, the workers become the central figure within the industrial landscape—the human presence at the heart of modern progress.

We wish to thank Professor Luis–Martín Lozano for his kind assistance in the research and cataloguing of the present work.Provenance:Private Collection, New Jersey.Lot Note:Diego Rivera strongly believed that the potential for political and social change in Mexico resided with children. For him, children were the future of Mexico, and as such played a notable role in his work beginning in the 1920s. Large-scale murals such as those at the Secretaría de Educación Pública and at the Alameda include peasant children participating in many of the scenes of everyday post-revolution life, but Rivera also featured children in smaller scale, tender portraits, such as the present work.When Cabeza de Niño was created in 1935, the artist was home in Mexico after his time in the United States working on the ill-fated Rockefeller mural, a very prolific period for him when he created numerous works with a mind toward generating income. This period coincided with a desire amongst American collectors for works by Mexican artists, so Rivera took advantage of this to support himself financially. Smiling out at the viewer, the children Rivera represented during this time symbolized for him the great potential of the next generation to create a future Mexican society, in a time of political transformation and social upheaval.

Pablo Picasso
(Spanish, 1881-1973)

The Picasso Administration has reviewed the present work and will issue a certificate of authenticity for it mid-November, 2026.We also wish to thank the Comité Madoura for confirming the authenticity of the present Lot, and acknowledging it is a unique piece outside of the numbered edition. Provenance:The Artist.The Estate of the Artist (Inventory Number 57901).Collection of Marina Picasso, the Artist's daughter. Private Collection. Note:In 1946, Pablo Picasso discovered in the pottery workshops of Vallauris a medium that would become an important part of his artistic practice. Through his collaboration with Suzanne and Georges Ramié at the Madoura workshop, he explored the possibilities of earthenware, transforming traditional vessels into expressive forms that blurred the boundaries between painting, sculpture, and the decorative arts. By modelling, incising, and painting directly onto clay, Picasso embraced the material’s versatility to create an extraordinary variety of faces, animals, and fantastical figures.Conceived in 1954, Vase Femme Pichet is based on the model catalogued by Alain Ramié as no. 236, Tête de Femme Couronnée de Fleurs, produced in two editions: an unglazed white version of 50 and a coloured version of 100. The present work is a unique prototype, distinguished by its exceptionally delicate, chiselled floral crown. Against the softly rounded face, whose features are defined by bold, gestural brushstrokes, the flowers emerge in vivid relief, their rich green, yellow, and blue glazes accentuated by touches of red. This striking contrast between the spontaneity of Picasso’s painted lines and the refined sculptural treatment of the crown gives the work its singular character.Women were a recurring subject throughout Picasso’s career, and ceramics offered him a particularly inventive means of exploring the female face. Often reduced to a few expressive marks, his ceramic portraits transform familiar features into playful, animated forms. Here, the floral crown lends the figure an almost regal presence, while its asymmetrical modelling preserves the spontaneity and vitality characteristic of his work in Vallauris.Only two comparable examples are known: one made for Suzanne and Georges Ramié themselves, and another held in the Design Museum Den Bosch in the Netherlands.

Auguste Rodin
(French, 1840-1917)
Femme au Pyjama Noir Entrouvert, c. 1900
watercolor and pencil on paper laid to board
signed Aug. Rodin (lower right)

Property from the Collection of Jules and Etta Mastbaum

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
The present work will be included in the forthcoming Catalogue raisonné des dessins et peintures d'Auguste Rodin (1840-1917) being prepared by Christina Buley-Uribe under the archive number 261002. Provenance:(Likely) Newman Galleries, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.Collection of Jules and Etta Mastbaum.By descent to the descendants of Jules and Etta Mastbaum.Exhibited:London, The Pastel Society, Piccadilly, W., The Galleries of theRoyal Institute of Painters, Third Annual Exhibition, June 17-July 20, 1901, cat. nos. 208-212 (for the entire group of drawings, exhibited under the title Working Drawings – A Spanish Dance), p. 36 (not illustrated), n. 11 on Sutro's photographic list (with the mention 300 francs).Lot Note: Executed in the late 1890s, this striking work belongs to the celebrated Femmes pyjama series, a group of just 14 watercolors that exemplify Auguste Rodin’s enduring and resolutely modern fascination with the female form.In each work, the sculptor depicts a single model (likely MademoiselleCamillot-Prévost, whom Rodin nicknamed "the little Spanish dancer") in subtly varied poses, her torso serving as the focal point of the composition. As she reveals her body by opening her pyjamas with either hand, she tilts her head from side to side and shifts her weight between her legs in a sinuous, undulating movement. The torso becomes the true subject of each drawing, its pearlescent luminosity contrasting with the dark contours of the garment. Rodin’s remarkable sensitivity to watercolor and delicate line lends depth and subtlety to the rendering of both flesh and drapery. Conceived as a series, these works reflect his interest in the fragmented body, reminiscing his fascination with antique sculpture. Viewed together, their torsos emerge at once, their individual forms merging into a striking visual rhythm.Distinguished by its large scale and exceptionally beautiful marbled effects, the present work is further notable for its exhibition history. It was among the few drawings from the series exhibited in London in 1901 at the Royal Institute Galleries, as part of an exhibition organized by the Pastel Society at the initiative of British artist Esther Sutro. Its provenance is equally distinguished: the watercolor belonged to Jules E. Mastbaum, the prominent Philadelphia collector and philanthropist whose celebrated collection formed the foundation of the city’s Rodin Museum. This exceptional Philadelphia provenance, combined with the work’s impressive scale and painterly effects, makes it a particularly compelling example of the series. As the Rodin expert and art historian Christina Uribe concludes, it is “undoubtedly one of the finest examples of its kind."

Francis in the Stable (Franziskus im Stall), 1927

We would like to thank Roswita and Viktor Pontzen, Archiv und Werkbetreuung Albert Birkle, Salzburg, for their research and kind support.Provenance:The Artist, until 1978.Neue Münchner Galerie, Munich, by 1980.Marvin and Janet Fishman Collection, Milwaukee.A gift from the above.The Cardinal Stritch University, Milwaukee.A gift from the above to the present owners.Exhibited:Berlin, Johannes Hinrichsen im Künstlerhaus Berlin, Bellevuestraße, Sonder-Ausstellung Albert Birkle, Sept. 3 - 30, 1927, no. 22.Berlin, Preußische Akademie der Künste zu Berlin, Frühjahrsausstellung, May - June 1928, no. 18.Tuttlingen, Germany, Kleine Galerie Stadt Tuttlingen, Albert Birkle, June - July 1979.Salzburg, Germany, Salzburger Museum Carolino Augsuteum, Albert Birkle, Ölmalerei und Pastell, July 11 - Sept. 7, 1980, no. 20, illustrated.Milwaukee, Milwaukee Art Museum, German Art 1909-1936: From Expressionism to Resistance, The Marvin and Janet Fishman Collection, Dec. 6, 1990 - Feb. 3, 1991, pp. 28-29; 164-165, no. 7, illustrated (erroneously dated to 1925; and traveling to Berlinische Galerie, Museum fur Moderne Kunst, March 1 - April 28, 1991; The Jewish Museum, New York, Nov. 21, 1991 - Jan. 25, 1992; Joslyn Art Museum, Omaha, Nebraska, Feb. 15 - April 19, 1992; High Museum, Atlanta, June 6 - Aug. 30, 1992).Literature:Listed in the digital catalogue raisonné by Roswita and Viktor Pontzen, Salzburg, under no. 772.Sylvia Kraker, Albert Birkle, 1900-1986, Ph.D. dissertation, Leopold-Franzens-University, Innsbruck, 1992, no. 653.Essay:Albert Birkle was born in Charlottenburg (later part of Berlin), Germany in 1900, and raised in a family of artists. His maternal grandfather and father were both painters, and Birkle grew up working as a decorative painter alongside his father, apprenticing at his company. In 1918, he attended the Hochschule für die bildenden Künste (College of Fine Arts) in Berlin, the present Universität der Künste, and studied with Arthur Kampf and Ferdinand Spiegel. Later, he joined the Berlin Secession and the Association of Berlin Artists in 1921, studying with Max Liebermann.Birkle was associated early in his career with the Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity) artists, a group which included George Grosz, Otto Dix, and Max Beckmann. The group formed during the Weimar Republic (1919-1933), the era between the two World Wars and before the rise of the Nazi Party. During this period, artists moved away from Expressionism and its visual language of Romanticism toward a realism they felt was more befitting of the new circumstances they faced in the aftermath of the First World War.While Birkle’s work did include some of the common themes of the group, portraits of workers and scenes of urban decay, he diverged from his counterparts by dedicating significant time to religious themes, particularly crucifixions, while still employing a style characterized by elongated, often malnourished-looking, haunting figures. In the post-World War II years, he made a living painting church murals and frescoes while living in Austria.In the present painting, Francis in the Stable (Franziskus im Stall) from 1925, Birkle places Saint Francis of Assisi in a barn surrounded by cows, a goat, and a horse, with only the glow from a high window behind him, and the saint’s small halo, to light the intimate scene. St. Francis lifts a finger to the viewer as well as to the animals, in instruction,benediction, or warning, as St. Francis understood all creatures to be children of God and therefore the brothers and sisters of man. Preaching humility, simplicity, and piousness, St. Francis sheds a single tear for humanity, for the ills of society.Birkle believed the artist had a responsibility to “bring something of the breath of a higher spirituality. It is no more than a very modest contribution, but it seems to me that the artist today is called upon more than anyone else—and I hope that he shall succeed with his meager powers—to preserve the human for humanity” (Pfefferkorn, Albert Birkle: Leben und Werk, 1983, p. 97).The painting was formerly part of the Marvin and Janet Fishman Collection, acquired during the artist’s lifetime from the Neue Münchner Galerie in Munich. The Fishmans later donated the work to Cardinal Stritch University, a school founded and sponsored by the Sisters of St. Francis of Assisi and the Franciscan religious order, which closed in 2023.

Robert Antoine Pinchon
(French, 1886-1943)
Le Jardin à Darnétal (La Tour Gothique de l'Église Saint Pierre de Carville à Darnétal)
oil on canvas
signed Robert Pinchon (lower right); signed again (on the reverse) and inscribed with artist and title (on upper stretcher)

The present lot will be included in the forthcoming online Pinchon Catalogue raisonné being prepared by Anne-Marie Letailleur, under number 1192. It is accompanied by a certificate of authenticity.Provenance:Private Collection, Westchester, New York, c. 1929-2019.By descent, Bluffton, South Carlina, 2019.Acquired from the above by the present owner, 2026.Lot Note:Robert Antoine Pinchon’s freshly rediscovered La Tour gothique de l’église Saint-Pierre de Carville à Darnétal captures the historic character of Normandy through one of the region’s most distinctive architectural landmarks. Located in Darnétal, just northeast of Rouen, the tower of Carville is a masterpiece of Flamboyant Gothic architecture, dating to 1525. Originally associated with the neighboring church of Saint-Pierre, it became a freestanding monument following a fire in 1562 during the Wars of Religion. Its richly articulated stonework and intricate Gothic ornament reflect the prosperity and artistic vitality of Normandy at the close of the Middle Ages. For Pinchon, the monument offered a subject in which the enduring presence of history could meet the changing effects of light and atmosphere. A leading figure of the second generation of the École de Rouen, Pinchon belongs to a distinguished tradition of artists who brought the principles of Impressionism and Post-Impressionism to the landscapes and towns of Normandy. Emerging in the late nineteenth century, the Rouen School was never a unified movement governed by a single aesthetic doctrine, but rather a succession of painters connected by their regional roots and their engagement with modern painting. Inspired in part by the example of Claude Monet and Camille Pissarro, artists including Charles Angrand, Joseph Delattre, Léon-Jules Lemaître, and Charles Fréchon explored the expressive possibilities of color, light, and painterly brushwork. Their successors, among them Pinchon and Pierre Dumont, carried this legacy into the twentieth century, incorporating bolder colors and increasingly liberated handling of paint. In this context, Pinchon’s depiction of the tower of Carville offers more than a picturesque view of a historic monument. It reflects the enduring dialogue between Normandy’s rich architectural heritage and the modern painter’s search for new ways of interpreting the visible world. By turning his attention to a familiar landmark near Rouen, Pinchon continues the regional tradition shaped by the Impressionists, reaffirming the central place of Normandy in the development of modern French landscape painting.

Henri Lebasque
(French, 1865-1937)
Nu Étendu, Bras Levés, Au Coussin Bleu, c. 1920-1921
oil on canvas
signed Lebasque (lower right)

25 3/4 x 32 in. (65.4 x 81.3 cm)

Property from The Estate of Arthur Schleifer, Jr., Boston, Massachusetts

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
This work was previously authenticated by Jean-Claude Bellier.Provenance:Galerie Hervé, Paris in 1969.Acquired directly from the above by the present owner. Exhibited:Paris, Galeries Georges Petit, Lebasque, March 11-30, 1927.Lot Note:Nu Étendu, Bras Levés, Au Coussin Bleu, c. 1920-1921, is a compelling example of the artist Henri Lebasque’s intimiste style. Born in Champigné, Lebasque went to Paris in 1885 to study art. He frequented the atélier of Léon Bonnat, the French painter, collector, and teacher at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts and befriended fellow students Pierre Bonnard and Edouard Vuillard, who would go on to establish the Nabis group. He was also influenced by the Intimists, who favored the calm and quietude of domestic subject matter. The theories on complimentary color by Seurat and Signac also left a lasting impact on Lebasque and remained essential to his technique throughout his life.In the 1920s, Lebasque increasingly focused on the depiction of female nudes in richly sumptuous interiors. Guided by his friend Henri Matisse, with whom Lebasque had founded the Salon d'automne in Paris in 1903, he developed an affinity for the depiction of lavish patterning in interior spaces. Lebasque painted at least three versions of the present composition, one of which currently resides in the Musée de Luxembourg. Nu Étendu, Bras Levés, Au Coussin Bleu depicts a languorous, voluptuous nude who reclines on a blue and white floral cushion, which strongly contrasts against the Middle Eastern and African textiles on which she lies. The use of these fabrics reflects the artist’s penchant for evoking exotic settings, while the tinges of green along the extreme edges of the woman's figure intimate at the wild use of color favored by Matisse and his fellow fauve painters.Of the nudes painted by Lebasque in the 1920s, Lisa A. Banner has written:[these nudes were] the culmination of [Lebasque's] intimist manner of painting--the celebration of the female form as fertile, warm, and inspiring...Matisse's nudes of the same period, painted in his neighboring villa on the Riviera, share his rich decorative sense, but approach the nude in a more intellectual style, as opposed to Lebasque's sensuous style. Lebasque painted his young models in poses of penetrating intimacy and subtle clarity (in Lebasque, exh. cat., Montgomery Gallery, San Francisco, 1986, pp. 70; 72).

description_block:
Maxime Maufra
(French, 1861-1918)
La Plage de Beg-Meil
oil on canvas
signed Maufra (lower left)

15 x 18 in. (38.1 x 45.7 cm)

Property from a Private Collection, South Carolina. 

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
The present lot is registered in the Archives Durand-Ruel under the number #29335. A photo-certificate signed by Caroline Durand-Ruel Godfroy and dated February 7, 2017 accompanies this lot.Provenance:Private Collection, Aury, acquired in the 1960s.Thence by descent.Christie's, London, sale of March 1, 2017, Lot 536 (as Plage aux Grands Arbres).Acquired directly from the above sale by the present owner.Lot Note:In his views of the Breton coastline, Maxime Maufra captured the untamed beauty of a landscape shaped by the ever-changing moods of the Atlantic. Situated near Fouesnant in southern Finistère, Beg-Meil is characterized by its rocky shores, sheltered coves, and emerald-green waters, a distinctive setting that attracted artists seeking to convey the powerful atmosphere of Brittany.In the present work, Maufra evokes the coast beneath a heavy, slate-grey sky, where the gathering clouds suggest the imminent arrival of rain. Tall trees frame the landscape, lending the composition a sense of shelter and verticality, while the vivid green of the sea provides a striking counterpoint to the somber tones overhead. This interplay between darkening skies and luminous coastal waters captures the particular character of the Breton seascape, where moments of tranquility are often charged with the promise of an approaching storm.A leading painter of Brittany, Maufra developed an individual style that combined the atmospheric sensitivity of Impressionism with a more assertive use of color and structure. Having encountered Paul Gauguin and the artists of the Pont-Aven circle, he remained deeply committed to painting directly from nature, exploring the changing effects of weather, light, and season along the Atlantic coast. In the present canvas, his expressive handling of the landscape conveys not simply a specific place, but the elemental poetry of Brittany itself.

Albert Marquet
(French, 1875-1947)
Femme Nue Debout dans un Atelier, c. 1900
oil on canvas
signed Marquet (lower left)

31 1/2 x 19 3/4 in. (80 x 50 cm)

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
The present lot is currently under review for authenticity by the Wildenstein-Plattner Institute, New York.Provenance: Collection of Marcelle Marquet, the Artist's widow. Private Collection, New York. Exhibited:Paris, Grand Palais, Les Indépendants à la Belle Époque, 1895-1901, March 25 - April 17, 1966, illustrated.Tokyo, Wildenstein Tokyo, Exposition Albert Marquet, June 19 - July 17, 1982, no. 6, illustrated.New York, Wildenstein, Albert Marquet, 1875-1947: A Tribute to the Late Jean-Claude Martinet, Author of the Forthcoming Catalogue Raisonné of the Artist's Work, April 10 - May 17, 1985, pp. 4; 89, illustrated (and traveling to London, Wildenstein, June 19 - July 31, 1985).Lausanne, Fondation de l'Hermitage, Albert Marquet, 12 February - 5 June 1988, no. 12.Lot Note:Albert Marquet likely painted the present nude at the home of his friend Henri Manguin, located at 61 rue Boursault in Paris’s Batignolles district. Purchased by Manguin in 1889, this charming residence became a gathering place for artists and musicians, hosting such figures as Claude Debussy, Maurice Ravel, Henri Matisse, and Marquet himself. The cropped head visible in the lower right of the composition may well belong to Manguin, offering a tantalizing glimpse into the intimate artistic circles in which Marquet moved.Marquet’s early nudes, executed between 1900 and 1910, offer a revealing insight into his artistic development, bridging the academic discipline of his training at the École des Beaux-Arts under Gustave Moreau and the radical experimentation of Fauvism. There, Marquet explored the human figure through simplified forms, expressive contours, and increasingly daring approaches to color and light. While retaining the close observation of the model characteristic of academic study, these works depart from conventional ideals of finish and idealization in favor of a more immediate, personal interpretation of the body. The present painting thus belongs to a particularly intimate and formative chapter in Marquet’s career, illuminating an aspect of his practice less familiar than the luminous harbor scenes and urban landscapes for which he is best known.

In the watercolor, the field comes alive with softly curved diagonal furrows that transition from luminous blue, to an earthy mauve, and then ultimately to soft ocher. With the blue fence that surrounds the house likewise reflecting the blue of the fields, all appear to be a chromatic mirror of one another. Lucien Lévy-Dhurmer
(French, 1865-1953)
Portrait of a Man, presumed to be Pierre Villey (1879-1933)
oil on canvas

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
We would like to thank Marc-Henri Tellier for confirming the authenticity of this work. It will be included in the Catalogue raisonné de l'œuvre de Lucien Lévy-Dhurmer currently in preparation. A certificate will be delivered to the buyer.Provenance:Barry Friedman, Ltd., New York. (label affixed to frame reverse, erroneously identifying the sitter as Edmond Rostand and with a date of c. 1905-1910.)Lot Note:The present portrait likely depicts Pierre Villey (1879-1933), a scholar of remarkable resilience. At the age of four, Villey became blind, but despite this, he pursued advanced studies, earning accolades at school and eventually passing the agrégation (a competitive examination for teaching positions) in literature, graduating first in his class. In 1908, he wrote his doctoral thesis on the philosopher and humanist Montaigne's Essays at the Theirs Foundation, outside of Paris. Les Essais de Michel de Montaigne, édition conforme au texte de l'exemplaire de Bordeaux was published by Villey in 1914, with another edition being published by Félix Alcan in 1922-23, reedited in 1924. In Lévy-Dhurmer's portrait, Villey holds his book as he intently stares above it into the distance. The diffused paint surface creates an almost dreamy atmosphere to the composition, as if the subject is lost within a scholarly world of his own.Villey was also famous for his dedication to the cause of the visually impaired, publishing several works on the world of the blind, which were translated into numerous languages. From 1924 until his death, he served as the Secretary General of the Valentin Haüy Association, an organization dedicated to the blind. Sadly, Villey died at the age of 54 on October 24, 1933, when the Caen-Paris express train he was on derailed.

Provenance: Richard Green Gallery, London.Acquired from the above by the present owner.Exhibited:London, Richard Green Gallery, Modern British Paintings, 1988 (image on poster advertising the exhibition)Lot Essay:Dame Laura Knight painted Children in a Rowboat in 1916, during a very productive period for the artist when she was living in the seaside town of Newlyn, England. She and her husband, the painter Harold Knight, moved to the coast at the behest of Stanhope Forbes a few years before, to join his artist’s colony. Both artists soaked in the sunlit seascape and relaxed lifestyle, and their work became more impressionistic as a result, particularly in the time before the beginning of World War I. Once the war broke out, the British government forbade artists from painting on the coastline, out of safety concerns, but Knight was able to secure a special permit to continue painting there.By the mid-1920s, Dame Laura Knight was a household name in Britain, in 1929 becoming the first female artist to be made a Dame of the British Empire. Her biographer Alice Strickland called her “a woman of firsts,” as she was also the first modern female artist to be elected to the Royal Academy (since Angelica Kauffman in the 18th Century) and the first to have a solo exhibition there. She went on to create a large and varied body of work, which included portraits, landscapes, intimate scenes of the ballet and circus, and later propaganda works during World War II. She famously obtained permission to attend the Nuremberg war crimes trials so that she could produce one of her best known paintings.Children in a Rowboat captures the energy and spirit of the next generation, right in the middle of the first World War. Despite the conflicts in the wider world, the boys strip down and swim off the boat, while the girls sit on the dock and chat in their frocks and hats. Like the artist, the children seem to be able to take small pleasures in daily life and to even find beauty during a most troubling time.

Born in Nantes, he began painting as a young man in his spare time, while working in his family’s business. In 1881 at the age of 20, Maufra’s parents encouraged him to travel to England to improve his English language skills, and there he came into contact with the atmospheric landscapes of Turner and Constable, which changed the course of his life and career. After returning to France, Maufra began dedicating more time to painting, increasingly en plein air, studying the changing effects of the light and atmosphere along the Loire. His inclusion in John Flornoy’s 1886 Impressionist exhibition, alongside Paul Gauguin, Claude Monet, Alfred Sisley, Camille Pissaro and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, solidified his position and attracted favorable attention from art critics.Maufra’s work continued to change through his connection with the artists of Pont-Aven and, particularly once he met Paul Gauguin in 1893. Maufra incorporated elements of Synthetism’s visual language, without fully embracing it, maintaining his own style outside of any defined school. Gustave Loiseau
(French, 1865-1935)
Rue de l'Hopital, Le Vaudreuil, 1913

signed Loiseau and dated (lower left)

We wish to thank Mr. Didier Imbert for kindly confirming the authenticity of the present lot, which will be included in the forthcoming Catalogue Raisonné of the artist's work, and accompanied by a certificate of authenticity.Provenance:The Artist.Galerie Durand Ruel, Paris, acquired from the Artist, November 11, 1913.Private Collection, France.David Findlay Gallery, New York, 1966.Sotheby's, New York, sale of February 18, 1988, Lot 25.Richard Green Gallery, London.Acquired directly from the above by the present owner.Lot Note:Illustrating a clear, bright day along a road in the village of Le Vaudreuil in Normandy, the present work is a superb example of Gustave Loiseau’s distinctly unique style, which he developed over many years of study. Considered one of the foremost post-impressionist painters, Loiseau was greatly influenced by the generation of impressionists who came before him, including Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, and Camille Pissarro. Born in Paris to parents who ran a successful butcher shop, Loiseau was apprenticed to a house painter and then to a decorator, which aroused his interest in art. In 1887, he received an inheritance from his grandmother that allowed him to study art full time. He briefly attended the Ecole des Arts Décoratifs and then studied under the landscape painter Fernand Just Quignon.As Loiseau was mostly self-taught, he shaped his style through close observation of nature and careful scrutiny of his impressionist forebears. Like them, he was a champion of painting en plein air, yet he developed his own artistic technique that used a distinct crosshatched brushstroke, called en treillis. This method created an evanescent quality and movement to his compositions and reveals the influence of pointillism in his work. As an admirer of the younger artist’s work, Claude Monet introduced Loiseau to the art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel, who signed an exclusive contract with him two years later. The resulting financial independence allowed the artist to journey throughout France to paint various landscapes, ranging from Normandy and Brittany in the north to Dordogne, in the southwest.Here, Loiseau has taken as his subject a charming road, Rue de l’Hopital, in the village of Le Vaudreuil. Nestled in the hollow of a valley and crossed by the river Eure, the artist depicted the village’s picturesque environs in several compositions. The vertical format of the present canvas, with the road centrally placed and leading towards two figures in the distance, creates a dynamic perspective. The medieval buildings enclose the space and create dark shadows that then dramatically open to the clear blue sky. Analogous to Monet, Loiseau explored in his canvases different atmospheric conditions caused by the surrounding landscape and bodies of water. The atmospheric clarity of the day is almost palpable, created using richly pigmented brushstrokes that scintillate across the surface in a careful patchwork of purples, blues, and ochres. This work masterfully highlights Loiseau’s experimental nature and his intuitive use of both impressionist and post-impressionist techniques to capture nature as it is experienced.

II, Paris, 1996, p. 211, no. 1133, illustrated.Lot Note:In the late 1920s, a woman claiming to be a German actress arrived in Paris with two men promoting an idea for a film, The Woman of the Hundred Faces, the premise involving a woman who had portraits painted by one hundred well-known artists, all capturing different aspects of her appearance and persona. They approached Jean Cocteau, who created the first portrait of Maria Lani, and then encouraged other artists and friends to participate in the project. Over fifty prominent artists heeded the call, inviting Lani to sit in their studios, including André Derain, Henri Matisse, Fernand Léger, Pierre Bonnard, Kees Van Dongen, Chaim Soutine, Man Ray, Marc Chagall, Giorgio de Chirico, Francis Picabia, Jules Pascin, Georges Rouault, Suzanne Valadon, Raoul Dufy, Charles Despiau, and Georges Braque.While the film never came to fruition, Lani and her companions collected the works into a traveling exhibition that began in November 1929 at the Brummer Gallery in Manhattan. Time Magazine reviewed the show, asking “Is she beautiful? Is she thin, fat, dropsical, anemic, senile, kittenish or reptilian? Last week Manhattanites asked these questions about Maria Lani, French cinemactress.” The collection later traveled to the Arts Club of Chicago; the Kunstkring, Rotterdam; Alfred Flechtheim Gallery, Berlin; Georges Bernheim Gallery, Paris; and Leicester Square, London. A limited-edition book was also published to commemorate the collection.In 1931 the actress who took the art world by storm and amassed a very valuable collection of paintings seemingly disappeared. A 2018 article in Vanity Fair by Brian Moynahan delved deeper into what actually became of her and the scam she perpetrated, outlining the international intrigue and eventual death of Lani in 1954.

We wish to thank Professor Luis–Martín Lozano for his kind assistance in the research and cataloguing of the present lot.Provenance:Christie's, London, sale of December 10, 1968, Lot 242.Acquired from the above sale by the family of the present owner.Exhibited:Exposición de Pintura y Escultura, [unknown gallery], Santa Clara Street, Mexico City, Mexico, May 7 - May 14, 1906, cat. no. 3 (organized by painter Gerardo Murillo for the Savia Moderna monthly art magazine).Lot Essay:Beginning his training at the age of eleven, Rivera attended drawing lessons at the Old Academy of San Carlos [Escuela Nacional de Bellas Artes], studying under some of the most renowned Mexican artists of the era such as Julio Ruelas, a distinguished Art Nouveau and Symbolist draughtsman, and the experienced Catalan Antonio Fabrés, who had recently become director of painting and implemented a new curriculum. Under Fabrés Rivera learned the scientific “Pillet Method,” developed by French artist Jules Jean Désiré Pillet, which emphasized real life observation over copying classical statues or lithographs. This 1906 rural scene, executed shortly before his departure to Europe, exemplifies Rivera’s drawing method grounded in direct observation. While only a few of these works were reviewed in contemporary newspapers and magazines, some have resurfaced over the past century, while others remain undiscovered. description_block:
Germaine Richier
(French, 1902-1959)
La Sauterelle, Moyenne, 1945
bronze with dark brown patina
signed G. Richier and numbered 6/8 (on base); also bearing a Valsuani foundry stamp (on base)

height: 20 3/4 in. (52.7 cm)

Property from The Estate of Arthur Schleifer, Jr., Boston, Massachusetts

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Provenance:Galerie Creuzevault, Paris.(Presumably) Galerie Hervé, Paris.Acquired directly from the above c. 1960.﻿Lot Note:Germaine Richier occupies a singular place in twentieth-century sculpture, transforming the human figure through a language of fragmentation, hybridity, and organic abstraction. Trained in the studio of Émile-Antoine Bourdelle, Richier developed an early mastery of the figure before moving, in the years surrounding the Second World War, toward increasingly strange and fantastical forms that merged human and animal anatomies. Her sculptures of the 1940s are populated by hybrid beings- part woman, part insect, bird, or plant- through which she challenged conventional ideals of beauty and the human form.Conceived in 1945, La Sauterelle, Moyenne belongs to this pivotal period and is among Richier’s most emblematic creations. The work depicts a crouching, grasshopper-like figure whose elongated limbs and angular body appear poised between stillness and sudden movement. Its anatomy is at once recognizably human and unmistakably insectile: the torso bends forward, the head rises from a heavily textured neck, and the long, attenuated limbs extend outward as though preparing to spring. Richier’s dark patina and roughly worked surface further blur the distinction between figure and natural material, giving the bronze the appearance of something excavated, weathered, or grown rather than conventionally modeled.The Sauterelle emerged from Richier’s fascination with the insect world, particularly the creatures she encountered in the landscapes of southern France. In her sculpture, these forms became vehicles for a broader exploration of metamorphosis and the instability of physical identity. The grasshopper, traditionally associated with lightness and flight, is rendered here as a powerful, earthbound presence: tense, angular, and almost skeletal. Its precarious balance creates a palpable sense of latent energy, as if the figure might at any moment spring from its base.La Sauterelle, Moyenne is particularly significant within Richier’s development, marking the emergence of the hybrid vocabulary that would become central to her mature practice. Richier produced three principal versions of the subject- the petite in 1944, the moyenne in 1945, and the grande in 1955–56- each exploring the tension between animal and human, stability and movement. The present sculpture is one of an edition of eight bronzes.In La Sauterelle, Moyenne, Richier transforms the familiar figure of the grasshopper into something at once primitive, uncanny, and profoundly alive. The work exemplifies her radical reimagining of the sculptural figure in the immediate postwar period, when the integrity of the human body itself had become a site of profound artistic and existential questioning. Rather than depicting the body as an idealized whole, Richier makes it unstable and metamorphic, suspended between human, animal, and natural forms. The result is a sculpture of remarkable physical tension- rooted to the earth yet seemingly ready to spring into motion.

El Lissitzky
(Russian, 1890-1941)
Proun (Schizzo), c. 1922-1923
gouache and pencil on paper
inscribed in Cyrillic with artist, title and medium (verso)

17 7/8 x 17 7/8 in. (45.5 x 45.5 cm)

Property from a Private Family Collection

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Exhibited:Bellinzona, Switzerland, Museo Villa de Cedri, Looking for Lissitzky, September 20, 2025 - January 25, 2026, no. 65.Literature:Carole Haensler, Lissitzky and Switzerland: Museo Villa dei Cedri, Bellinzona, Zurich : Verlag Scheidegger & Spiess, 2026, p. 77, no. 65 (illustrated).Lot Note:Conceived by El Lissitzky in 1919, Proun, an abbreviation of Project for the Affirmation of the New, became one of the defining experiments of the Russian avant-garde. Blurring the boundaries between painting, architecture, and design, the series explored how abstract forms could occupy and transform space, establishing a new visual language that would inform Lissitzky’s work across multiple disciplines.Developed in dialogue with Kazimir Malevich’s Suprematism, Proun moved beyond the autonomous geometric forms of the earlier movement toward a more dynamic conception of pictorial space. In the present work, rectangles, discs, and jutting axes appear to advance, recede, intersect and rotate, creating an impression of movement and structural tension within the two-dimensional surface. Rather than depicting a recognizable subject, Lissitzky here constructs an imagined environment in which balance, orientation, and spatial relationships remain in constant flux. Color serves not merely as a decorative element but as an essential means of distinguishing planes and articulating their relationships, allowing the composition to suggest three-dimensional construction without abandoning the flat surface of the work.Through its restrained palette of blue, white, and gray the works lends a sense of depth and shifting perspective, while its square format reinforces the impression of a self-contained yet potentially expansive spatial system.

description_block:
Paule Gobillard
(French, 1867-1946)
Jeune Fille au Chapeau de Paille dans le Jardin à Givry, Bourgogne, 1898
watercolor and pencil on paper

sheet: 10 5/8 x 7 5/8 in. (27 x 19.4 cm)

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
We would like to thank Mme Dominique d'Arnoult for her assistance with the authentication and cataloguing of the present lot.Provenance:Eric Gillis Fine Art, Brussels (as by Julie Manet (French, 1878-1966) and titled Portrait de Paule Gobillard en Extérieur, 1897).Acquired from the above, 2017.Lot Note:Young Girl in a Straw Hat in the Garden at Givry, Burgundy, 1898 is by Paule Gobillard, niece of Berthe Morisot (1841-1895). Gobillard received her training as a painter alongside her aunt, who referred her to Henri Gervex to acquire the fundamentals of the craft. It was as Gervex's student that she began exhibiting at the Salon de l’Union des femmes peintres et sculpteurs. In 1891, Gobillard exhibited for the first time at the Salon des Indépendants, which she continued to do until 1912. She entered the Salon d'Automne in 1904 and exhibited there regularly until her death in 1946.The present composition can be compared to Gobillard’s painting of the same subject, titled The Straw Hat, 1898 (Paris, Aguttes, sale of November 28, 2024, Lot 33). In both the watercolor and the painting, the model, who wears the same dress and hat in both, is seated in a garden before a landscape opening onto the horizon and sky. She touches the brim of her hat and is seemingly lost in contemplation. A bouquet of red flowers sits on her lap and provides a bright focal point at the center of the composition.The watercolor can also be compared to another watercolor, signed with Paule Gobillard's initials and dated P. G. / 1898 (Paris, Beaussant-Lefèvre, sale of May 5, 2023, lot 200, as Jeannie Valéry and Jeanne Baudot in the garden at Louveciennes). The work, now faded, has been mistakenly located at Jeanne Baudot's home in Louveciennes (Julie Manet does not mention such a stay in her journal in 1898). More likely, it illustrates a stay at the Deanery of Givry, in Burgundy, described at length by Julie from August 25 to September 7, 1898 in her journal. Under the guidance of their new friend Jeanne Baudot—whom their painting teacher Pierre-Auguste Renoir had introduced to them—Julie and her cousins ​​Jeannie and Paule Gobillard were invited to the Clément home. Both watercolors illustrate the same landscape in the background, the same tree silhouette, the same palette, and the same paper size, which seem to indicate the same date and location.It is not strictly speaking a portrait, but a figure that may have been painted from one of the young women present in the household, perhaps Jeanne Clément, a pianist and student of Pugno, whose "Marie Antoinette-style sheer kerchief over a pinkish-orange dress," they admired (Julie Manet, Journal, August 27, 1898). Paule Gobillard then revisited her watercolor, painted from life, to create a studio painting intended for exhibition. Pierre-Auguste Renoir had taken over from his friend Berthe Morisot regarding the artistic education of young women after Morisot’s death in 1895. The art of watercolor, here characterized by its delicacy and transparency, is part of the development of the eye.
